newsitem.title: UK: Britain's CWS turns up heat on predator Regan.
newsitem.headline: Britain's CWS turns up heat on predator Regan.

text.p: Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) on Tuesday turned up the heat on predator Andrew Regan by referring concerns about a previous deal between the two parties to Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO).
"We have now formally drawn this situation to the attention of the SFO," a CWS spokesman told Reuters, adding that City law firm Linklaters & Paines had visited the SFO to voice CWS' concerns.

But an SFO spokeswoman told Reuters the office -- responsible for investigating and prosecuting frauds over a million pounds -- was not investigating the affair sparked by the billion pound plus takeover bid by an offshoot of Regan's Lanica Trust.

Earlier 31-year-old entrepreneur Regan and his associates won an 18-hour reprieve from a London High Court order requiring him to disclose any confidential information he may have about the 153-year-old supermarkets to funeral parlours group.

The order had also required Regan, Lanica, its offshoot Galileo Group, Lanica director and former CWS adviser David Lyons and a senior CWS manager Allan Green to provide sworn affidavits by 1500 GMT on Tuesday detailing what information they had.

Last Thursday CWS suspended Green and another senior CWS executive David Chambers for an alleged serious breach of trust. It has admitted to hiring private investigators to monitor the activities of Regan, Lyons and Green.
Regan has been stalking CWS since February when it first emerged that Galileo was interested in the Co-op's non-food businesses.
Galileo admitted last Friday that it intended proposing that the mutually-owned group convert to a limited company which it would then buy.
The predators are believed to have the profitable Co-operative Bank in their sights and Ireland's Allied Irish Banks has admitted it would be interested in buying it.
Retailer Sainsbury has declined to comment on speculation that it would buy some of the CWS retail outlets. Galileo is also expected to hive-off the Co-operative Insurance Society.
CWS dates back to a group of artisans called the Rochdale Pioneers who banded together in 1844 in Lancashire, north west England to set up a retail shop selling pure untainted food to working people.

The latest twist to the takeover saga, which the CWS has said it will vigorously defend, concerns a follow-up supply deal to the buy-out in 1994 of the CWS food manufacturing group by Hobson Plc. Regan was chief executive of Hobson, which later sold on the business at a substantial profit.

Graham Melmoth, CWS chief executive, has expressed concerns to Regan and his advisor Hambros Bank about a payment of 2.4 million pounds ($3.9 million) to a third party in connection with the extension of the original supply deal.

Regan responded to Melmoth's questions on Tuesday and said the payment formed part of a legitimate transaction which had been in the best interests of Hobson. Melmoth replied saying he was still not satisfied with the explanations and carried out his threat to inform the SFO.

In an unrelated development it emerged late on Tuesday that the London-based arm of Japanese securities giant Nomura is also involved in the CWS takeover bid. A Nomura spokesman told Reuters that the firm had been preparing to provide Galileo with debt financing for its proposals.

Banking sources said Nomura would continue to support the bid team with its offer of 1.2 billion pounds in financing facilities if legal obstacles are removed. But given Regan's success in obtaining a court extension, the legal process is not expected to be completed before Friday.
This means the details of the Galileo proposals, which must overcome significant internal barriers within the CWS structure, are unlikely to surface in the near future, sources said.

One suggested that in addition to the 1,000 pounds which Galileo has been rumoured ready to offer to the hundreds of thousands of individual Co-op members to accept the takeover, it is also ready to make a one-off payment of 10-15.0 million pounds to good causes currently supported by the CWS.

Despite the problems being encountered by Regan and his team, banking sources said the Co-op was now "in play" for a takeover. "If Regan and Galileo do not go for it, someone else will," said one source, adding that there was significant hidden value among the CWS businesses. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
